text: With my review about the original Deus Ex and now this review for Invisible War, you’d think I have something against the series. I’m giving these games a shot but lost interest in both very quickly. This time I could barely make it to an hour and a half before calling it quits. There are some echoed statements from my previous review, including: +Default mapping of buttons is pretty nonsensical. +Uninteresting story +Bad voice acting I didn’t find the new HUD to be that bad and the enemy AI has definitely been improved over the first game. Invisible War also follows the original with a seemingly good amount of story and things to uncover that flesh out the plot. I used the Unified Texture Pack mod and widescreen support utility. Those 2 combined did make the game look good for its age, even at 1440p. The loading points are a bit strange. It will drop back to the desktop, flash a white screen and then reload. This takes a good 10 seconds or so and can be irritating. I’m 0-2 for liking Deus Ex games…but I’m hoping Human Revolution will snap me out of it.

title: deus ex: invisible war
text: If You think about playing DX:IW there is a good chance that You came across its older brother, DX. Either You hated it because at first glance the options were overwhelming, playing it like a shooter was hard and frustrating or loved it for its complexity, the richness of the world, the great storytelling. Either way, there are good news and bad news for You. I was one of those who disliked DX:IW when it came out. This was the time of a new console generationt and these swallowed a large proportion of the gaming community - and this was one of the first games the developers clearly created with console gamers in mind. This meant that the user interface was oversimplified and blocked half of the view, that the game was not properly optimized for PC, that the creators had to settle for smaller level size or decreased game complexity. All the above meant that in the eyes of most PC gamers DX:IW was an unbecoming second installation to its truly amazing predecessor. I played it through then halfheartedly, and then again and again with more and more enthusiasm. Now, 10 years later I will summarize my opinion as I see this game today, sometimes in comparison with DX. First our old grievances: - 10 years passed, so the lack of optimization is not an issue anymore, - there are community packs to make it look bettter, looks good for its age, - smaller levels meant more loading (game settings were broken up into smaller levels) but with today's PCs this only takes a moment - also not a problem anymore, - hud can be customized via mods. Bad that did not change (a matter of taste, for You all these can be aadvantagious): - still oversimplified: awkward inventory management, less augmentations, no skill system, universal ammo is stupid, less background info through holomail or newspapers, etc, - male protagonist looks and sounds like a member of a boy band, - stealth gaming style does not always work - no-kill approach does not work (in DX it was only one person You really had to kill to advance in the story) Good that will remain good til the end of times (some of these I have learnt to appreciate only on my subsequent walkthroughs): - somehow the writer(s) managed to incorporate all three DX game endings into the sequel, so whichever ending You are familiar with, You will easily find Your bearings and understand the premise, - sidequests are fun and inspired, - new augs (though fewer) are fun to use, - similarly the new weapon mods are useful and fun, - great level design means that most of the time You still can choose between covert or guns-blazing approach, - one of the best intros of its time, - great NPC additions like the OMAR or NG Resonance, - amazing places to visit like Antarctica, Trier or Cairo (including an arcology building which looks good and feels right) All in all in my eyes funnily enough with age the game got better. It might feel disappointing after playing DX (or liberating, if You like less complexity), but a great game on its own right. Where DX gets A+++, DX:IW is worth an A- easily. Recommended.

title: deus ex: invisible war
text: I'm so happy that I went back and played Invisible War again after so many years. When I installed all I really had was a few sketchy memories about a couple of plot twists, coupled with smiles about my first experience with marijuana and ragdoll physics. By the end though, it was clear that I had been playing a game that, despite the outdated textures and AI, still beats many of the modern-day FPS shooters hands down in every important aspect. What I mean by that, is that Invisible War delivers an excellent plot with multiple endings and engrossing moral choices; often comical side missions, that stay well within the realms of possibility, leading to increased immersion while giving the player a little change-up from the main "Spy-spy-genocide-jihad" storyline - interestingly, something Human Revolution fails to do and is less of a game for it; and the abilty to access it all playing whichever way you want. Want to sneak? Cool bro, go for it. Want to burn people alive and laugh at them while they run around screaming? Go nuts. Want to just beat everyone into a bloody pulp and then throw the bodies off a building into a skip bin? (Is me fave) Well you can do that too! Invisible War also has many features modern shooters (and I can't understand why) don't include. Modifying my guns is A MUST for me in any action game, and Invisible War delivers, not only that, it gives you a legitimate ability to be non-lethal and still have a number of weapons and abilities at your disposal. So many things in this game are done better than in many later games that you really get the feeling it's still superior. This game (not franchise) is one of the best of all time for me - easily on par with the likes of Morrowind in terms of execution. Perfectly balanced gameplay.

title: deus ex: invisible war
text: [NO SPOILERS] If ever there was a game that was judged by association, this it it. More than anything, Invisible War is judged by the Deus Ex in it's name. Before it is even installed, it is expected to be at least as good and preferably better than one of the greatest games of all time. Hardly fair odds. As a result many people don't see anything other than the fact that Invisible War is not the same as the original Deus Ex. It doen't get a chance to stand on it's own and be judged on merit. It's like starting a music career by being told that if you don't do better than The Beatles, you are a complete failure. IMO Invisible War should be seen not as the sequel to Deus Ex, but as a different game in the same universe. The was Thor is not a sequel to Iron Man, but simply a different film set in the same universe. While there are many of the same themes and elements, the end products are not the same. If judged on it's own merit, Invisible War is a pretty great game. Sure, the levels are small, but they are well designed and offer many gameplay options. The shooting is competent. Much better than it ever was in Deus Ex. Controls are well above most games of it's time. It's no secret that many things were dumbed down from Deus Ex. While I do prefer the old, more advanced system which gave more player options, the new, simpler system is perfectly functional. And given the in-game time gap between the two games, such changes can easily be explained by technological development. Just look at the difference in weapons from WW1 to WW2. One major point that divides people is the universal ammo. Personally, I think it's interesting. While it doesn't make much logical sense that all types of weapons would use the same ammo, it does bring something new to the game. Since different weapons use different amounts of ammo with each shot, inventory management becomes more important. Especially for people like me who in most games are used to just using the pistol 95% of the time and therefore always having plenty of ammo for the big guns. In Invisible War you can't just squirrel away lots of ammo for the big guns and save it for the big enemies. Now you actually have to plan ahead from time to time. While it's not a system I would like to see widely used in games, I do find it interesting. Bottom line: I personally think Invisible War is a very solid game. It is unfairly judged by it's association with a game it could never live up to. Take it as a single game and judge it on it's own merit. Do that and you will likely find that it is much better than people give it credit for. In fact, it is very good game.

title: deus ex: invisible war
text: I really tried to like this game, but after numerous playthroughs, I just can't. Not only is the game - by far - not finished, it's almost completely broken. I mean, practically everything that made the first Deus Ex good has disappeared. The large open levels from the first game were replaced with small, closed levels. A walk from one level-change door to the next takes less than a minute on all levels in the whole game! The only thing that prolongs them are conversations and enemies, of which you can either skip or run past. While load times has been reduced due to the advancement of computers overall, they were a real pain when DXIW was first released. The story, and/or the world, has been transformed from the cyberpunk future of the previous game to some kind of anachronistic sci-fi future. Explanations are almost nonexistant. For instance, in 20 years since the Collapse (i.e. the end of the previous game), somehow, a weapons manufacturer managed to completely take over the global market AND develop universal ammo for all those weapons. Yet, airports do not exist or have been transformed to garbage dumps, people have stopped driving cars (or bicycles, or any other vehicle except helicopters). How was this possible? The story isn't all that bad, but the smallness of the game makes it too big. There simply isn't room enough for exploration or any meaningful sidequests. The choices you make are also pointless, since loyalty is changed back and forth at the slightest wrongdoing, and, as another reviewer said, the missions you get are practically all "kill this person or let it live". The character you play, as well as the game's NPCs, are almost all irritating fools. The voice acting is ridiculous, and the only two characters I liked were JC Denton and Luminon Saman, them also being the only two characters in the game who have anything interesting to say. The player, Alex D., have been made into an idiot, because it seems that he/she accepts anything another character tells him/her. Now, I know this was due to saving space to crunsh it inside an old X-Box console, but at least let the player read a datacube (which can store documents and so on). Parallell this with JC Denton's skepticism in the first game. Game mechanics are almost completely broken. Characters have to spin their whole body to face you straight on when they talk - even in a conversation between three people, and for EVERY new sentence. Something seems to be wrong with their eyes, because many NPCs look like they're on drugs. Combat is the only way forward. Want to sneak past an enemy or stun him in the back, like the previous game? Forget it. Get the "silent running" biomod if you want any sneaking, otherwise they will hear you miles away. Besides, where are you going to sneak about? The levels are too small for any kind of "Thiefing" around. Civilians become enemies without you ever touching them, even though they don't attack, but still. Why wasn't this refined for final release? Skill points are gone, and so are the choices of augmentations. Now there are biomods, and they are everywhere. You can also swap biomods at any point in the game, so it's not like your choice really matters. Besides, about halfway through the game, you have to use rocket launchers, sniper rifles or energy weapons to get anywhere, or you won't stand a chance against the enemy. Miss the techo-esque music from the first game? Too bad, it's now replaced with ambience. Some band, represented by NG Resonanse, also made it to the game, but they failed after like five songs (I think they were called "Three Faced" or some such). Now, I have no quarrel with ambience, or especially ambient game music (just listen to Fallout 1 & 2 soundtracks, for instance, or Mass Effect soundtracks). But imagine The Elder Scrolls soundtrack being replaced with, say, Viking rock or death metal, playing constantly? Not very moody. So, is it all that bad? Well, the game is certainly playable. The graphics are pretty neat, but that can't be a "positive" aspect of the game, because games do evolve. New engines are developed. It comes "naturally" if you will. It's just like aging, it happens, people grow up, get jobs, whatever. Of course it will have better graphics. The funny thing is, would it be better if they had reused the Unreal 1 graphical engine? I think yes. It would certainly fit more content. It would be "ugly", but hey, Wasteland 1 is "ugly". Fallout 1 & 2 are "ugly". System Shock 2, the Thief series. That doesn't mean they are bad games. In any case, get Deus Ex: Human Revolution instead. While it is a prequel, it is a good one in my opinion. Is Invisible War the worst game ever created? Of course not. But it certainly is not anything like the first game, or even close to the prequel. Oh, wait, there is one good thing about this game - how to not make a sequel. Game developers should definitely try this game then, after playing the first one. The sad thing is that if they had just waited for a couple more years, just until X-Box 360, this game could probably have been better. So; not recommended.

title: deus ex: invisible war
text: Deus Ex: Invisible War is a solid game with a great story, more focused on the action that the first part and simplifying the elements that were in this. PROS : - Continues and closes the storyline of the first part - Possibility to choose between a male or female protagonist with different options on their physical appearance. - Like the first part, what begins as a simple story unfolds in a story full of twists and complexities. - Like its predecessor, depending on the choices you make, you can change the style of the narrative or the relationship of certain NPC's toward the protagonist. - Is set on a Semi-Open World structure ala Wolfenstein (2009) for its narrative. - The exploration remains key for obtaining items, ammunition, rewards, etc. - Implementation of Havok Physics to move obstacles, hide corpses, attack, etc. - Multiple primary and secondary objectives to meet - Like the first part, there are multiple ways to meet the goals, reach a destination, get an item, etc. - Augmentations obtained and improved can be replaced by others once installed. - Integration of an ability to climb certain surfaces becomes quite useful. - Being a game more focused on the action than the first part, the combat is much more polished than its predecessor (Though the element of stealth is still present). - Most of the ranged weapons have a secondary fire mode. - Very good textures and lighting effects for its time CONS : - The protagonist, whatever male or female, does not have enough charisma. - Most NPC's share the same face. - Many elements are simplified when compared to its predecessor (No experience points for improve character skills, all guns share the same ammunition, many fewer weapons, the tool for hacking and lockpicking is the same one, etc.). - Improvements of the characters are limited exclusively to augmentations (As long as you have the item that allows you to install or upgrade these). - Each weapon only accept two modifications (From a total of eight options). - Control over jumps is sometimes a bit disastrous. - Many times, the use of physics in certain situations, is erratic and not let the situation settle directly or at the first attempt (Which can be a bit frustrating ). - The Quick-Load is not so "Quick". - The campaign lasts half the first Deus Ex (We are talking about a campaign of approximately 30 hours, although this is much more than the average for today's games). - An annoying Black-Screen bug present in the final length of the game when you load a Savegame

title: deus ex: the fall
text: This was a nice game that certainly shows promise, the acting is a little bit..erm..."B"...grade, but if you look past it, the storyline is definately there. This game is too short and leaves a massive cliff hanger at the "end" telling you there will be more to come (when, what, why???). follows the Human revolution skill tree style for your augmentations, but seems limited in comparison. this may only be because of the length of the game (its a $10 or less game). If your looking for a taste of the Deus Ex franchise this game is certainly a nice but subtle taste of the world. You will find the morals and ethics of Augmentation described very well, with more insight into the "human" aspect of augmentation. I would like to rave on about how this would give insight into what the future could be like, but there is just not enough meat on the bone of this game (not like Human Revolution) but with some more "episodes" this should turn out well. The combat is okay, but slams it home that regardless of your Characters "skills" and background, going in guns blazing is almost never a good idea, you can manage fairly well if you have cover and the right gun, but stealth and non-lethal measure seem to be the key to getting things done. You aim is terrible until you get the Augmentation for both aim and recoil, but upping your cloke and silent running seems to be more effective, and as long as you have the energy, a takedown is more effective anyway. I will not harp on too much more, as the rest can be decided by yourself. I do recommend this game, but take it with an open mind and do not expect AAA game dev, but this is a nice little look into the world of Deus Ex as it currently stands. 6/10

title: dishonored
text: One of the most fascinating games I've played in a long time. Often stealth games don't allow for complete stealth, instead forcing unavoidable combat at various points (Sniper games, for example). This one does not do that. You can try to "Ghost" your way through, or you can try to just kill everyone. But beware, the latter method has far reaching consequences that can be quite unpleasant. The graphics are just a bit rough, but forgivable given the story and the gameplay. Some powers do seem rather strong, but even those have their flaws to keep it interesting. I like open world games, but this is not one of them. It is quite flexible in the paths to the goal, but you are pretty much proceeding to the goal withing a fairly limited zone, whichever path you take. Didn't matter, there were enough nooks and crannies to investigate, and the lore picked up on the way enriches the game's world/story. As with many games, there are repetitive lines that get annoying. But listening to the dialogue that does not get repeated adds yet more lore. Actual combat is also somewhat repetitive, but I guess there is only so much one can do in a sword fight, though they don't let you do half of it. When I had to kill, I preferred the variety of stealth methods. Direct combat can be cut short with a pistol, but that gets a lot of attention. However, the blink skill make it possible to escape even during a fight. Nonlethal seems to have limits, you are either shooting a sleep dart, which leaves a body to deal with, or you have to come up from behind them and execute a chokehold. There's a timer to tell you when your victim is unconscious from a choke, but while you are choking him, you are unable to drag him back out of sight or do anything else. Time it out wrong, and some one is going to see you. I am sure that I will eventually find all the possible paths to the various goals, but until I do, this is a game well worth playing again and again. The characters are quirky, and fairly unique in my experience. I can recommend the game for anyone who prefers to be sneaky rather than overtly aggressive.

title: divinity ii: developer's cut
text: A tl;dr to start -------------------- Pros: Great lines, great lore, a solidly long campaign. Cons: Frustrating gameplay, unintuitive progression and a ridiculous waste of potential Overall: If you took the 'game' out of this game, it would be stellar. -------------------- Divinity has always been strong with story and the world really nets any player willing to immerse themselves. But I am time and again flung right back out when I find myself fighting the game itself instead of enemies, puzzles or the like. A myriad of problems ranging from punishingly steep character progression costs, many quests requiring an hour or more of searching for a button in a badly lit room or being forced to trudge through huge enemy level jumps. The game is meant to be difficult, but there is a difference between punishing a wrong choice and requiring the player to save every few seconds for fear of being trapped in an area twice their level. It is a roller coaster of geart narratives, hilarious and deep characters, and heaps of dissapointment. For every heartfelt chuckle or legitimate moment of curiousity I had there was a moment or three of a frustrated sigh, loading the last save and trying once again to complete some menial task or fight. There were a few moments where the narrative progression almost made it all worth it, but sadly the game's peaks do not outweigh its trenches. Worst of all, the second bit (Flames of Vengeance) greeted the player with a choice, end sequence and resolution that, to put it quite blunty, felt like it was pulled from the nearest rancid pile of trash, slapped on for the sake of completion. I am incredibly dissapointed to not recomend this game, as the world, characters and overall plot are some of the best I've seen in a fantasy RPG. But the fumbling in basic gameplay, design and simply the actual 'game' bits of this title ruin it as an overall experience.

title: divinity ii: developer's cut
text: I owned the xbox version before I bought it on steam. Probably have 200+ hours in that. One of only two Focus Interactive games that I actually like. This is an almost unique blend of action, wonder, well thought out gameplay and even a bit of humor that allow the player to immerse themselves in the story, the lore, the thrill that you get when you finally beat a really tough stage. This is an example of what can happen when the devs listen to the players and adjust thier games accordingly. You see this was one of the products of what I call the Golden Age of gaming 2007-2013. If you look closely, this does not have, lootboxes, pointless DLC's, paywall content, microtransactions or just about any moneygrubbing tactic used by the likes of Unbisoft or EA these days. This does not try to be a Dark Souls wannabe, it is its own game. Yes there are a couple of niggles, early glitches were common, and save corruption ruined many a game. Also the steam version does not have Controller support because, well I really don't know why exactly. The point is that the devs, wait for it, fixed the bugs! They did not just say "Deal with it"-Farcry 2 or "The problems were addressed in the new DLC we are releaseing"- ME3. Yes the graphics do feel dated to us now but this is the best you will get for some magic hack and slash action without having to pay through the nose. Look, don't take my word for it, buy the dang thing. Keep Larian liquid so they can save the world from EA.

title: divinity ii: developer's cut
text: When I bought the Divinity Anthology, I was really just buying it for this game (but I still soldiered through Divine Divinity at least first before jumping to this one). It was worthwhile playing through Divine Divinity - there's a lot of little callbacks and references to the world and previous events that made the experience of Divinity 2 more enjoyable. Divinity 2 is a 3rd person Action RPG with a skill tree and stat allocation - think like a combination of World of Warcraft and Diablo. My wife said it reminded her of Dark Souls (or at least watching me play it) and I can see the resemblance. Overall the system works well - it's got a nice skill basis such that you can dodge around projectiles and attacks and avoid using potions and even kite enemies around if you're ranged. The options for character customization are broad too. The world is large and full of character, and they definitely improved the quality of voiceover from Beyond Divinity. The plot is solid with an interesting (but apparently controversial) ending. Unfortunately it does fall into the trap of 'throw dozens of enemies at them' again, with the endgame becoming a -bit- of a trudge. They do close it out with a solid final area though. The expansion pack sold the game for me though. They took the enemy count, toned it down, and made the majority of it venturing through one town fixing problems, talking to people, solving puzzles. One giant series of side quests, essentially. It was executed really well - and then they nailed the final sequence out of the park. Playing through the first two Divinity games to get to Divinity 2 was definitely worth the wait - and I'd even recommend picking it up outside of the anthology if you don't care about the world-building done by the previous two games.
